name: Shimcache
location: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache (Windows 2003 and later); HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatibility\AppCompatCache on Windows XP/2000. Values are held in memory and only periodically flushed to the registry, typically on shutdown.
purpose: Part of the Application Compatibility infrastructure: when Windows evaluates whether an executable needs a compatibility shim, it records the file's path, size, and last-modified time in a cache so it doesn't have to re-evaluate the file on every launch. Because the cache captures files the OS has looked at, it's used as evidence a given executable existed (and, on some versions, ran) on the system.
key_fields: $STANDARD_INFORMATION last-modified timestamp of the file (NOT a run time)
File size (present on some Windows versions)

Process Execution Flag: present on Windows Vista, 7, Server 2008, and Server 2012 only; TRUE indicates the entry reflects actual execution, FALSE indicates the file was merely referenced (e.g. via directory browsing by the Application Experience Lookup Service) without running
Cache entry position/order (reflects last-update order, exploited for approximate sequencing)
normal_baseline: A large list of legitimate OS and application binaries with last-modified timestamps matching their known install/patch dates, generally clustered around Windows Update and application install events; entry order roughly tracks last-referenced order rather than true execution order.
anomalies: Entry for an executable in a Temp, Downloads, or other user-writable path with a last-modified timestamp inconsistent with any known legitimate install
On Windows Vista/7/2008/2012, an entry with the Process Execution Flag set to TRUE for a binary in a suspicious location. A stronger indicator of actual execution than presence alone

A single-use or renamed binary appearing once with no corresponding Prefetch, Amcache, or event-log evidence of execution. Consistent with a tool that was staged/inspected but not run, or with an execution artifact that was separately cleared

Timestamp manipulation: because the cached time is the file's $STANDARD_INFORMATION last-modified value (attacker-controllable via timestomping), a suspiciously 'clean' or backdated last-modified time on a malicious binary should be cross-checked against $FILE_NAME timestamps or other artifacts
anti_forensic_notes: Critical version-dependent caveat: Shimcache reliability as proof of execution has changed across Windows releases. On Windows XP/2003 there is no execution flag at all, so presence alone was historically treated as a rough proxy for execution. On Windows Vista, 7, Server 2008, and Server 2012 a Process Execution Flag was added that distinguishes actual execution (TRUE) from mere presence, e.g. directory browsing (FALSE), though Mandiant notes the flag's true internal semantics were never officially documented by Microsoft. On Windows 8 and later the execution-flag behavior changed again and is widely reported as unreliable/removed, meaning an entry can exist for a file that was never executed. Because of this, Shimcache should never be used alone to prove execution on modern Windows. Always corroborate with Prefetch, Amcache, or BAM/DAM. The cache itself lives in memory and is only flushed to the registry hive periodically (typically at shutdown), so a hard power-off can lose recent updates, and clearing/rebuilding it requires kernel-level access rather than a simple deletion.
